questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3}+{y}^{2},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & ∗ \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3} & {x}^{3}+3x{y}^{2}+2y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}6xy & 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & 6xy+2\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+3+(x-1)=2x+1.
$$

questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ ∗\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ ∗\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ ∗\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+y}+2x & \frac{1}{x+y}+3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+2 & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+6y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+4+(y-1)+(y-1)+5+(y-1)=3y+7.
$$

For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & =3, & \,{f}^{′}(1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =3, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & ≈3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3+(-2)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+\frac{1}{2}(4) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,-1) & =-e, & \,{f}^{′}(1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-e, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & ≈-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-e+2e+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}e \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =e+\frac{1}{2}(-e+1) \\  & =\frac{e+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,-1,-1) & =4, & \,{f}^{′}(2,-1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(2,-1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(1,0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =4, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈4+[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,0) & ≈4+[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4+[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4+1+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =5+\frac{1}{2}(-3) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
